 Part 1 READING PASSAGE 1 You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13 which are based on Reading Passage 1. 

 Radio Automation
 Today they are everywhere. Production lines controlled by computers and operated by robots. There’s no chatter of assembly workers, just the whirr and click of machines. In the mid-1940s, the workerless factory was still the stuff of science fiction. There were no computers to speak of and electronics was primitive. Yet hidden away in the English countryside was a highly automated production line called ECME, which could turn out 1500 radio receivers a day with almost no help from human hands. 
 A . John Sargrove, the visionary engineer who developed the technology, was way ahead of his time. For more than a decade, Sargrove had been trying to figure out how to make cheaper radios. Automating the manufacturing process would help. But radios didn’t lend themselves to such methods: there were too many parts to fit together and too many wires to solder. Even a simple receiver might have 30 separate components and 80 hand-soldered connections. At every stage, things had to be tested and inspected. Making radios required highly skilled labour—and lots of it.
 B . In 1944, Sargrove came up with the answer. His solution was to dispense with most of the fiddly bits by inventing a primitive chip—a slab of Bakelite with all the receiver’s electrical components and connections embedded in it. This was something that could be made by machines, and he designed those too. At the end of the war, Sargrove built an automatic production line, which he called ECME (electronic circuit-making equipment), in a small factory in Effingham, Surrey.

 C . An operator sat at one end of each ECME line, feeding in die plates. She didn’t need much skill, only quick hands. From now on, everything was controlled by electronic switches and relays. First stop was the sandblaster, which roughened the surface of the plastic BO that molten metal would stick to it The plates were then cleaned to remove any traces of grit The machine automatically checked that the surface was rough enough before sending the plate to the spraying section. There, eight nozzles rotated into position and sprayed molten zinc over both sides of the plate. Again, the nozzles only began to spray when a plate was in place. The plate whizzed on. The next stop was the milling machine, which ground away the surface layer of metal to leave the circuit and other components in the grooves and recesses. Now the plate was a composite of metal and plastic. It sped on to be lacquered and have its circuits tested. By the time it emerged from the end of the line, robot hands had fitted it with sockets to attach components such as valves and loudspeakers. When ECME was working flat out; the whole process took 20 seconds.

 D . ECME was astonishingly advanced. Electronic eyes, photocells that generated a small current when a panel arrived, triggered each step in the operation, BO avoiding excessive wear and tear on the machinery. The plates were automatically tested at each stage as they moved along the conveyor. And if more than two plates in succession were duds, the machines were automatically adjusted—or if necessary halted In a conventional factory, I workers would test faulty circuits and repair them. But Sargrove’s assembly line produced circuits so cheaply they just threw away the faulty ones. Sargrove’s circuit board was even more astonishing for the time. It predated the more familiar printed circuit, with wiring printed on aboard, yet was more sophisticated. Its built-in components made it more like a modem chip.
 E . When Sargrove unveiled his invention at a meeting of the British Institution of Radio Engineers in February 1947, the assembled engineers were impressed. So was the man from The Times. ECME, he reported the following day, “produces almost without human labour, a complete radio receiving set. This new method of production can be equally well applied to television and other forms of electronic apparatus.

 F . The receivers had many advantages over their predecessors, wit components they were more robust. Robots didn’t make the sorts of mistakes human assembly workers sometimes did. “Wiring mistakes just cannot happen,” wrote Sargrove. No w ừ es also meant the radios were lighter and cheaper to ship abroad. And with no soldered wires to come unstuck, the radios were more reliable. Sargrove pointed out that the drcuit boards didn’t have to be flat. They could be curved, opening up the prospect of building the electronics into the cabinet of Bakelite radios.
 G . Sargrove was all for introducing this type of automation to other products. It could be used to make more complex electronic equipment than radios, he argued. And even if only part of a manufacturing process were automated, the savings would be substantial. But while his invention was brilliant, his timing was bad. ECME was too advanced for its own good. It was only competitive on huge production runs because each new job meant retooling the machines. But disruption was frequent. Sophisticated as it was, ECME still depended on old- fashioned electromechanical relays and valves—which failed with monotonous regularity. The state of Britain’s economy added to Sargrove’s troubles. Production was dogged by power cuts and post-war shortages of materials. Sargrove’s financial backers began to get cold feet.

 H . There was another problem Sargrove hadn’t foreseen. One of ECME’s biggest advantages—the savings on the cost of labour—also accelerated its downfall. Sargrove’s factory had two ECME production lines to produce the two c ữ cuits needed for each radio. Between them these did what a thousand assembly workers would otherwise have done. Human hands were needed only to feed the raw material in at one end and plug the valves into then sockets and fit the loudspeakers at the other. After that, the only job left was to fit the pair of Bakelite panels into a radio cabinet and check that it worked.
 I . Sargrove saw automation as the way to solve post-war labour shortages. With somewhat Utopian idealism, he imagined his new technology would free people from boring, repetitive jobs on the production line and allow them to do more interesting work. “Don’t get the idea that we are out to rob people of then jobs,” he told the Daily Mnror. “Our task is to liberate men and women from being slaves of machines.”
 J . The workers saw things differently. They viewed automation in the same light as the everlasting light bulb or the suit that never wears out—as a threat to people’s livelihoods. If automation spread, they wouldn’t be released to do more exciting jobs. They’d be released to join the dole queue. Financial backing for ECME fizzled out. The money dried up. And Britain lost its lead in a technology that would transform industry just a few years later.

 Part 2 READING PASSAGE 2 You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26 which are based on Reading Passage 2. 

 The Cacao: A Sweet history
 A Chapter 1 
 Most people today think of chocolate as something sweet to eat or drink that can be easily found in stores around the world. It might surprise you that chocolate was once highly treasured. The tasty secret of the cacao (Kah Kow) tree was discovered 2,000 years ago in the tropical rainforests of the Americas. The story of how chocolate grew from a local Mesoamerican beverage into a global sweet encompasses many cultures and continents.

 B Chapter 2 
 Historians believe the Maya people of Central America first learned to farm cacao plants around two thousand years ago. The Maya took cacao trees from the rainforests and grew them in their gardens. They cooked cacao seeds, the crushed them into a soft paste. They mixed the paste with water and flavorful spices to make an unsweetened chocolate drink. The Maya poured the chocolate drink back and forth between two containers so that the liquid would have a layer of bubbles or foam.
 Cacao and chocolate were an important part of Maya culture. There are often images of cacao plants on Maya buildings and art objects. Ruling families drank chocolate at special ceremonies. And, even poorer members of society could enjoy the drink once in a while. Historians believe that cacao seeds were also used in marriage ceremonies as a sign of the union between a husband and a wife.

 The Aztec culture in current-day Mexico also prized chocolate. But, cacao plants could not grow in the area where the Aztecs lived. So, they traded to get cacao. They even used cacao seeds as a form of money to pay taxes. Chocolate also played a special role in both Maya and Aztec royal and religious events. Priests presented cacao seeds and offerings to the gods and served chocolate drinks during sacred ceremonies. Only the very wealthy in Aztec societies could afford to drink chocolate because cacao was so valuable. The Aztec ruler Montezuma was believed to drink fifty cups of chocolate every day. Some experts believe the word for chocolate came from the Aztec word “xocolatl” which in the Nahuatl language means “bitter water.” Others believe the word “chocolate” was created by combining Mayan and Nahuatl words.

 C Chapter 3 
 The explorer Christopher Columbus brought cacao seeds to Spain after his trip to Central America in 1502. But it was the Spanish explorer Hernando Cortes who understood that chocolate could be a valuable investment. In 1519, Cortes arrived in current-day Mexico. He believed the chocolate drink would become popular with Spaniards. After the Spanish soldiers defeated the Aztec empire, they were able to seize the supplies of cacao and send them home. Spain later began planting cacao in its colonies in the Americans in order to satisfy the large demand for chocolate. The wealthy people of Spain first enjoyed a sweetened version of chocolate drink. Later, the popularity of the drink spread throughout Europe. The English, Dutch and French began to plant cacao trees in their own colonies. Chocolate remained a drink that only wealthy people could afford to drink until the eighteenth century. During the period known as the Industrial Revolution, new technologies helped make chocolate less costly to produce.

 D Chapter 4 
 Farmers grow cacao trees in many countries in Africa, Central and South America. The trees grow in the shady areas of the rainforests near the Earth’s equator. But these trees can be difficult to grow. They require an exact amount of water, warmth, soil and protection. After about five years, cacao trees start producing large fruits called pods, which grow near the trunk of the tree. The seeds inside the pods are harvested to make chocolate. There are several kinds of cacao trees. Most of the world’s chocolate is made from the seed of the forastero tree. But farmers can also grow criollo or trinitario cacao plants. Cacao trees grown on farms are much more easily threatened by diseases and insects than wild trees. Growing cacao is very hard work for farmers. They sell their harvest on a futures market. This means that economic conditions beyond their control can affect the amount of money they will earn. Today, chocolate industry officials, activists, and scientists are working with farmers. They are trying to make sure that cacao can be grown in a way that is fair to the timers and safe for the environment.

 E Chapter 5 
 To become chocolate, cacao seeds go through a long production process in a factory. Workers must sort, clean and cook the seeds. Then they break off the covering of the seeds so that only the inside fruit, or nibs, remain. Workers crush the nibs into a soft substance called chocolate liquor. This gets separated into cocoa solids and fat called cocoa butter. Chocolate makers have their own special recipes in which they combine chocolate liquor with exact amounts of sugar, milk and cocoa fat. They finely crush this “crumb” mixture in order to make it smooth. The mixture then goes through two more processes before it is shaped into a mold form.
 Chocolate making is big business. The market value of the yearly cacao crop around the world is more than five billion dollars. Chocolate is especially popular in Europe and the United States. For example, in 2005, the United States bought 1.4 billion dollars worth of cocoa products. Each year, Americans eat an average of more than five kilograms of chocolate per person. Speciality shops that sell costly chocolates are also very popular. Many offer chocolate lovers the chance to taste chocolates grown in different areas of the world.

 Part 3 READING PASSAGE 3 You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 28-40 which are based on Reading Passage 3. 

 Extinct: the Giant Deer
 Toothed cats, mastodons, giant sloths, woolly rhinos, and many other big, shaggy mammals are widely thought to have died out around the end of the last ice age, some 10,500 years ago. 
 A 
 The Irish elk is also known as the giant deer (Megaloceros giganteus). Analysis of ancient bones and teeth by scientists based in Britain and Russia show the huge herbivore survived until about 5,000 B.C. – more than three millennia later than previously believed. The research team says this suggests additional factors, besides climate change, probably hastened the giant deer’s eventual extinction. The factors could include hunting or habitat destruction by humans.
 B 
 The Irish elk, so-called because its well-preserved remains are often found in lake sediments under peat bogs in Ireland, first appeared about 400,000 years ago in Europe and Central Asia. Through a combination of radiocarbon dating of skeletal remains and the mapping of locations where the remains were unearthed, the team shows the Irish elk was widespread across Europe before the last “big freeze.” The deer’s range later contracted to the Ural Mountains, in modern-day Russia, which separate Europe from Asia.
 C 
 The giant deer made its last stand in western Siberia, some 3,000 years after the ice sheets receded, said the study’s co-author, Adrian Lister, professor of palaeobiology at University College London, England. “The eastern foothills of the Urals became very densely forested about 8,000 years ago, which could have pushed them on to the plain,” he said. He added that pollen analysis indicates the region then became very dry in response to further climatic change, leading to the loss of important food plants. “In combination with human pressures, this could have finally snuffed them out,” Lister said.
 D 
 Hunting by humans has often been put forward as a contributory cause of extinction of the Pleistocene megafauna. The team, though, said their new date for the Irish elk’s extinction hints at an additional human-made problem – habitat destruction. Lister said, “We haven’t got just hunting 7,000 years ago – this was also about the time the first Neolithic people settled in the region. They were farmers who would have cleared the land.” The presence of humans may help explain why the Irish elk was unable to tough out the latest of many climatic fluctuations – periods it had survived in the past.
 E 
 Meanwhile, Lister cast doubt on another possible explanation for the deer’s demise – the male’s huge antlers. Some scientists have suggested this exaggerated feature – the result of females preferring stags with the largest antlers, possibly because they advertised a male’s fitness – contributed to the mammal’s downfall. They say such antlers would have been a serious inconvenience in the dense forests that spread northward after the last ice age. But, Lister said, “That’s a hard argument to make because the deer previously survived perfectly well through wooded interglacials [warmer periods between ice ages].” Some research has suggested that a lack of sufficient high-quality forage caused the extinction of the elk. High amounts of calcium and phosphate compounds are required to form antlers, and therefore large quantities of these minerals are required for the massive structures of the Irish Elk. The males (and male deer in general) met this requirement partly from their bones, replenishing them from food plants after the antlers were grown or reclaiming the nutrients from discarded antlers (as has been observed in extant deer). Thus, in the antler growth phase, Giant Deer was suffering from a condition similar to osteoporosis. When the climate changed at the end of the last glacial period, the vegetation in the animal’s habitat also changed towards species that presumably could not deliver sufficient amounts of the required minerals, at least in the western part of its range.
 F 
 The extinction of megafauna around the world was almost completed by the end of the last ice age. It is believed that megafauna initially came into existence in response to glacial conditions and became extinct with the onset of warmer climates. Tropical and subtropical areas have experienced less radical climatic change. The most dramatic of these changes was the transformation of a vast area of North Africa into the world’s largest desert. Significantly, Africa escaped major faunal extinction as did tropical and sub-tropical Asia. The human exodus from Africa and our entrance into the Americas and Australia were also accompanied by climate change. Australia’s climate changed from cold-dry to warm-dry. As a result, surface water became scarce. Most inland lakes became completely dry or dry in the warmer seasons. Most large, predominantly browsing animals lost their habitat and retreated to a narrow band in eastern Australia, where there were permanent water and better vegetation. Some animals may have survived until about 7000 years ago. If people have been in Australia for up to 60 000 years, then megafauna must have co-existed with humans for at least 30 000 years. Regularly hunted modern kangaroos survived not only 10 000 years of Aboriginal hunting, but also an onslaught of commercial shooters.
 G 
 The group of scientists led by A.J. Stuart focused on northern Eurasia, which he was taking as Europe, plus Siberia, essentially, where they’ve got the best data that animals became extinct in Europe during the Late Pleistocene. Some cold-adapted animals, go through into the last part of the cold stage and then become extinct up there. So you’ve actually got two phases of extinction. Now, neither of these coincide – these are Neanderthals here being replaced by modern humans. There’s no obvious coincidence between the arrival of humans or climatic change alone and these extinctions. There’s a climatic change here, so there’s a double effect here. Again, as animals come through to the last part of the cold stage, here there’s a fundamental change in the climate, reorganization of vegetation, and the combination of the climatic change and the presence of humans – of advanced Paleolithic humans – causes this wave of extinction. There’s a profound difference between the North American data and that of Europe, which summarize that the extinctions in northern Eurasia, in Europe, are moderate and staggered, and in North America severe and sudden. And these things relate to the differences in the timing of human arrival. The extinction follows from human predation, but only at times of fundamental changes in the environment.

fields.sentence:
1. Phân tích câu phức (Passage 1 - Đoạn C): 'The plate whizzed on. The next stop was the milling machine, which ground away the surface layer of metal to leave the circuit and other components in the grooves and recesses.'
- Cấu trúc: Mệnh đề quan hệ 'which ground away...' bổ nghĩa cho 'the milling machine'.
- Dịch nghĩa: Tấm bảng lao nhanh đi. Điểm dừng tiếp theo là máy phay, máy này mài đi lớp bề mặt kim loại để lại mạch điện và các linh kiện khác trong các rãnh và hốc.

2. Phân tích câu phức (Passage 3 - Đoạn E): 'High amounts of calcium and phosphate compounds are required to form antlers, and therefore large quantities of these minerals are required for the massive structures of the Irish Elk.'
- Cấu trúc: Câu phức với liên từ chỉ kết quả 'and therefore'.
- Dịch nghĩa: Một lượng lớn các hợp chất canxi và phốt phát là cần thiết để hình thành gạc, và do đó một lượng lớn các khoáng chất này là cần thiết cho những cấu trúc khổng lồ của loài nai khổng lồ Ireland.
fields.tips:
1. Dạng bài điền từ (Summary Completion): Chú ý giới hạn số lượng từ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS hoặc NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS). Đọc kỹ đoạn văn để tìm từ gốc (bản sao chính xác).
2. Dạng bài True/False/Not Given: 'NOT GIVEN' thường xảy ra khi câu hỏi đề cập đến một thông tin có liên quan nhưng bài đọc không khẳng định hay phủ định.
3. Dạng bài Flow-chart (Chocolate making): Đọc theo trình tự các bước trong quy trình. Chú ý các từ chỉ thời gian hoặc hành động (Then, After, Finally).
4. Dạng bài Matching People/Statements (Part 3): Cần tìm tên nhà khoa học hoặc nhóm nghiên cứu, sau đó tìm động từ (suggests, states, argues) để ghép với nhận định tương ứng.

fields.grammar:
Task 1:
- Cấu trúc chỉ xu hướng: 'While milk production in the Netherlands and Australia remained relatively stable or fluctuated, both Tanzania and Guatemala witnessed a continuous upward trajectory.'
- Cấu trúc so sánh: 'In stark contrast to the high-volume output of developed nations, Tanzania and Guatemala produced significantly lower quantities, yet their growth rates were more impressive.'
- Cấu trúc tóm lược: 'Overall, there is a clear dichotomy in production trends: established producers showed stagnation or decline, whereas emerging nations saw consistent growth.'
Task 2:
- Mệnh đề nhượng bộ: 'Although parental involvement in scheduling children's activities can ensure educational and developmental benefits, it risks stifling their autonomy and creativity.'
- Cấu trúc đảo ngữ: 'Not only does free play foster independence, but it also allows children to explore their unique interests and passions.'
- Cấu trúc lập luận: 'What is vital is a balanced approach where parents provide guidance rather than rigid control, allowing children the agency to select their own pursuits.'

Task 1:
The table provides data on the annual milk production in the Netherlands, Australia, Tanzania, and Guatemala over three years: 1990, 2000, and 2010.

Overall, the figures reveal a sharp divide in production trends between the two established producers and the two emerging nations. While the Netherlands and Australia produced high volumes of milk with fluctuating or declining output, Tanzania and Guatemala experienced consistent, strong growth, albeit starting from much lower levels.

In 1990, the Netherlands and Australia dominated the table, with production figures of 11,262,000 and 11,246,000 litres, respectively. By 2010, the Netherlands saw a slight increase in production, reaching 11,466,000 litres. Australia, however, witnessed a significant decline, with output falling to 9,165,000 litres after peaking at 11,105,000 litres in 2000.

In contrast, Tanzania and Guatemala began with relatively small outputs in 1990, at 87,000 and 26,000 litres. Over the next two decades, both nations experienced substantial growth. Tanzania’s production nearly doubled to 155,000 litres by 2010. Guatemala’s growth was even more pronounced, rising from 26,000 to 84,000 litres, more than tripling its original output by the end of the period.


Task 2:
The question of whether parents should dictate their children’s free-time activities or grant them the autonomy to choose is a common topic of parenting debate. While structured parental guidance provides stability and focus, I believe that children benefit more when given the freedom to choose their own recreational pursuits.

Proponents of parent-organized activities argue that structured time is essential for a child’s development. In an increasingly competitive world, parents often feel that every hour must be productive. By enrolling their children in music lessons, sports, or academic tutoring, parents ensure that their offspring gain skills that may be useful later in life. Furthermore, parental organization acts as a safeguard, ensuring that children spend their leisure time in safe, supervised, and beneficial environments rather than engaging in sedentary or potentially harmful behaviors.

Conversely, providing children with the freedom to choose their own activities fosters independence and intrinsic motivation. When children decide for themselves how to spend their leisure time, they learn how to navigate choices and accept the consequences of those decisions. This autonomy is crucial for self-discovery; it allows children to identify their unique interests and passions, which is arguably more important than the pursuit of 'useful' skills chosen by others. Moreover, children who are constantly managed by their parents often experience burnout or resentment, which can diminish their enthusiasm for learning and creativity.

In my opinion, the ideal approach is one of 'guided autonomy'. Parents should certainly expose their children to a wide array of options and provide the necessary support, but they should avoid micromanaging the child's schedule. A balance can be struck by establishing basic ground rules regarding productivity and safety, while leaving the final decision on how to enjoy the time to the child. This prepares them for adulthood, where decision-making skills will be paramount.

In conclusion, while the intention behind parent-led activity scheduling is often rooted in a desire for the child’s success, it can inadvertently suppress personal growth. Granting children the freedom to choose their own pastimes is essential for cultivating a well-rounded and independent individual.

### Part 1 Outline:
- Q1: Yes, absolutely. Public spaces offer a sense of community. 
- Q2: Essential. Parks act as green lungs for concrete jungles, aiding mental health.
- Q3: Tried once during the lockdown. It was rewarding but required high maintenance.
- Q4: Mildly reserved initially, but open if the stranger is polite and has good vibes.

### Part 2 Outline (A.R.E.A):
- **Answer (Where, When, Why):** An high-end audio store called 'Kỳ Audio' in Hanoi, visited last March to buy premium JBL home speakers.
- **Reason & Example (What happened):** The staff didn't just push the most expensive model. They asked about my room size, acoustics, and preferred genre (jazz/acoustic). They went the extra mile by setting up a dedicated soundstage and letting me test multiple Treble Neo configurations for over an hour. 
- **Alternative/Evaluation:** Unlike other pushy salesmen, they prioritized my experience over a quick sale. That customer-centric approach is rare and made me a loyal customer.

### Part 3 Outline:
- Q1: Mostly electronics, cosmetics, and food & beverage (F&B) venues.
- Q2: To share genuine experiences (both good and bad) and to help the community make informed choices.
- Q3: Yes, a double-edged sword. Good for transparency, but risky due to fabricated reviews.
- Q4: Extremely taxing. It requires emotional resilience and active listening.
- Q5: Agree. Due to the rise of social media and high expectations of instant gratification.

### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **Do you like visiting public places? Why or why not?**
Yes, definitely. I find public places like libraries and plazas highly inviting because they foster a strong sense of community. Being surrounded by the hustle and bustle of urban dwellers helps me feel connected to the city's pulse, which is a great way to unwind after a hectic day.

2. **Do you think it is important to have public parks in cities?**
Undoubtedly. Recreational green spaces act as the 'green lungs' of modern concrete jungles. They offer citizens an escape from the choking air pollution and provide a serene environment for physical exercise, which is paramount for both physical and mental well-being.

3. **Have you ever tried growing vegetables?**
To be honest, I tried my hand at growing organic tomatoes on my balcony during the lockdown, but I quickly realized I don't possess a green thumb. It was a high-maintenance endeavor that required daily monitoring, and unfortunately, my harvest was quite meager.

4. **How do you feel when a stranger strikes up a conversation with you?**
Initially, I might feel a bit caught off guard as I tend to value my personal space. However, if they are polite and approachable, I am more than happy to reciprocate and engage in some light-hearted small talk. It can actually be a refreshing way to broaden one's perspective.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
Last March, I had an absolute blowout experience at a boutique audio store named 'Kỳ Audio' located in the heart of Hanoi. I went there specifically to purchase a high-quality speaker system for my living room, as I wanted to upgrade my home entertainment setup.

What blew my mind was the staff's exemplary customer service. Instead of resorting to typical pushy sales tactics, the consultant took a highly personalized, customer-centric approach. He inquired in detail about my living room's dimensions, wall acoustics, and my personal music taste—which leans heavily toward acoustic and jazz. He then went the extra mile by setting up a dedicated soundproof booth, allowing me to test different models, including some sophisticated systems featuring Treble Neo configurations. He patiently explained the subtle nuances of each soundstage for over an hour.

I believe this service was truly outstanding because the staff prioritized my long-term satisfaction over making a quick, expensive sale. Their technical expertise, coupled with genuine patience, made me feel valued. Thanks to their guidance, I walked away with the perfect pair of speakers, and this stellar experience completely secured my loyalty to their brand.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **What kinds of things do people write online reviews about in your country?**
In Vietnam, people are highly vocal about tech gadgets, cosmetics, and culinary experiences. E-commerce platforms like Shopee and social apps like TikTok are inundated with feedback on everything from smartphones to local street food stalls, as consumers rely heavily on peer peer-to-peer recommendations before spending money.

2. **Why do some people write online reviews?**
Generally, it stems from a desire to share one's genuine experience. Some do it out of altruism—to help fellow shoppers avoid low-quality products or to praise a brand that went the extra mile. On the other hand, some write reviews to vent their frustration after receiving sub-par service, using it as a tool to hold businesses accountable.

3. **Do you think that online reviews are good for both shoppers and companies?**
Yes, but it is a double-edged sword. For shoppers, it provides unprecedented transparency and helps them make informed purchasing decisions. For companies, positive reviews serve as free word-of-mouth marketing, while constructive criticism can help improve their offerings. However, the system can be corrupted by fabricated reviews, which mislead consumers and unfairly tarnish a company's reputation.

4. **What do you think it might be like to work in a customer service job?**
I imagine it is a highly demanding role that takes a massive emotional toll on workers. Customer service representatives constantly operate in a high-pressure environment where they must deal with irate or unreasonable clients. It requires a high level of empathy, active listening, and the rare ability to keep one's cool under intense pressure.

5. **Do you agree that customers are more likely to complain nowadays?**
I absolutely agree. In this digital era, consumers have developed a craving for instant gratification and hold extremely high expectations. When a service falls even slightly short of perfection, they can easily voice their grievances instantly on social media, making complaints far more visible and frequent than in the past.

### Part 1 Outline:
- Q1: Hanoi, Vietnam. A vibrant, culturally rich capital city with a unique blend of historical charm and modern development.
- Q2: Yes, currently renting a cozy high-rise apartment. Love the security, modern amenities, and panoramic city views.
- Q3: Convenience is key. 24/7 security, gym, pool, and maintenance services are often a stone's throw away, plus it is highly cost-effective.
- Q4: Absolutely. It is a form of active meditation. Definitely planning to go on more long walks, specifically hiking trails, to escape the concrete jungle.

### Part 2 Outline (A.R.E.A):
- **Answer (Where, When, Who):** Ha Giang loop in Northern Vietnam, visited last autumn with a group of close university friends.
- **Reason & Example (Activities & Feelings):** We rented motorbikes to traverse the winding mountain passes. We feasted our eyes on majestic limestone peaks, deep valleys, and golden terraced rice fields. We actively engaged with the local ethnic minority children, learned about their culture, and enjoyed traditional corn wine by the fire.
- **Alternative/Evaluation:** Had we opted for a commercial resort, we would have missed the raw, untouched beauty of nature and the profound sense of serenity that this place offered. It completely recharged my batteries and changed my perspective on life.

### Part 3 Outline:
- Q1: Generally prefer rural or suburban areas due to the slower pace of life, cleaner air, and peaceful surroundings, though some value urban healthcare access.
- Q2: Massive strain on public infrastructure, resulting in severe gridlock, housing shortages, and deteriorating environmental quality.

### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **Where do you live?**
I currently reside in Hanoi, which is the bustling capital of Vietnam. It is a vibrant metropolitan area known for its rich tapestry of historical heritage blended seamlessly with rapid modern development.

2. **Do you live in an apartment? Do you like living there?**
Yes, I do. I am living in a high-rise apartment on the twentieth floor. I thoroughly enjoy it because it provides top-notch security, panoramic views of the city skyline, and isolates me from the relentless street-level traffic noise.

3. **Why do many people like living in an apartment?**
I believe the main appeal lies in convenience and security. Modern complexes offer integrated amenities like fitness centers, swimming pools, and convenience stores just a stone's throw away. Additionally, 24/7 security systems offer peace of mind, especially for young professionals with hectic schedules.

4. **Do you enjoy going for a long walk? Do you think you will try to go for a long walk in the future?**
Indeed, I do. Going for a long walk is like a form of active meditation for me; it is a brilliant way to declutter my mind. I am definitely planning to go on longer trekking trips in rural areas in the future to escape the concrete jungle and reconnect with nature.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
I would love to share my experience visiting Ha Giang, which is undoubtedly one of the most picturesque and awe-inspiring mountainous provinces in Northern Vietnam. I traveled there last autumn, right during the harvest season, alongside three of my closest friends.

During our four-day trip, we rented semi-automatic motorbikes to traverse the legendary, winding mountain passes, including the famous Ma Pi Leng. The primary activity was sightseeing, and we literally feasted our eyes on towering limestone peaks and deep valleys filled with golden terraced rice fields. We also hiked down to the Nho Que River, where we did some kayaking along the emerald-green water, looking up at the majestic canyon walls. In the evenings, we stayed at a local homestay, shared traditional meals with ethnic minority families, and learned about their rich cultural heritage.

This journey was absolutely unforgettable because the sheer scale of the landscape made me feel incredibly small yet profoundly connected to nature. It was the perfect destination to escape the hustle and bustle of city life, allowing us to fully recharge our batteries. The untouched, raw beauty of Ha Giang left a permanent mark on my mind, and I still look back at those serene moments whenever I feel overwhelmed by daily life.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **Do older adults prefer living in larger cities or rural areas?**
Generally speaking, elderly citizens lean toward living in rural or suburban areas. This preference is largely driven by the desire for a slower pace of life, cleaner air, and tighter-knit communities. However, some older adults do choose to remain in major cities, primarily due to the immediate proximity of state-of-the-art healthcare facilities, which become increasingly critical as they age.

2. **What are the main problems associated with overpopulation in urban areas?**
Overpopulation puts an immense strain on existing municipal infrastructure. The most prominent issue is severe traffic gridlock, which dramatically increases commute times and air pollution. Furthermore, the skyrocketing demand for housing leads to a high cost of living and the proliferation of substandard high-density living spaces, which can severely diminish the overall quality of life.

3. **What measures need to be taken by governments to make cities more livable?**
To breathe new life into overcrowded cities, governments must adopt a multi-faceted approach. First, they should invest heavily in expanding sustainable public transport networks, such as metro systems, to discourage private vehicle usage. Second, prioritizing green initiatives by incorporating more public parks and urban forests is essential. Lastly, decentralizing economic activities by developing satellite cities can effectively curb urban sprawl and distribute the population more evenly.

  * Be careful with the glottal stop or linking /r/ in *towering_limestone* and *soaring_altitudes*.

### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **Where is your hometown? Do you like living there?**
My hometown is Hanoi, the bustling capital of Vietnam. I absolutely adore living here because of its vibrant energy, historical charm, and the incredible street food scene, which is always a great source of pride for local residents.

2. **What is your favorite flavor of ice cream? Why?**
I would say my absolute favorite is matcha or high-quality dark chocolate. I am not a big fan of overly sugary treats, so I prefer flavors with a slightly bitter, sophisticated undertone that offer a more refined gastronomic experience.

3. **Do you think learning a foreign language is important?**
Undoubtedly. In this globalized era, mastering a foreign language does not just enhance your career prospects; it radically broadens your horizons by allowing you to connect with different cultures on a much deeper, more empathetic level.

4. **What is the most difficult part of learning a new language for you?**
For me, the most challenging aspect is always internalizing the intricate colloquial expressions and natural intonation. While grammar and vocabulary can be memorized through deliberate practice, speaking like a native requires a deep, intuitive grasp of cultural nuances.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
I would love to tell you about a book that has had a profound impact on my life and one that I find myself returning to at least once a year. It is the world-renowned novel "The Alchemist," penned by the brilliant Brazilian author Paulo Coelho.

At its core, the book is a beautiful, allegorical fable that follows the journey of an Andalusian shepherd boy named Santiago. He travels from his homeland in Spain to the Egyptian desert in search of a physical treasure buried near the Pyramids. Along the way, he encounters various mentors, including an alchemist, who teach him to listen to his heart, read the omens of the universe, and, most importantly, follow his own "Personal Legend."

I enjoy reading this book repeatedly because of its timeless philosophical wisdom. Every time I pick it up, especially when I am facing a major transitional phase or a difficult decision in my life, I discover a new layer of meaning. Coelho’s writing style is incredibly simple yet poetic, making it a compelling page-turner that never feels dry. Whenever I lose myself in this book, it serves as a powerful reminder that the journey itself is far more valuable than the destination, and it instantly recharges my mental batteries.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **Do Vietnamese people read a lot of books? What genres? Why?**
Generally speaking, the reading culture in Vietnam is undergoing a significant renaissance, particularly among the younger generation. While the general population might not read extensively compared to some Western nations, tech-savvy youth are increasingly consuming books. Popular genres lean heavily toward self-help, business strategy, and foreign literature. This is primarily because young people are highly driven by self-improvement and entrepreneurial ambitions, seeking actionable knowledge to succeed in a competitive market.

2. **Between e-books and physical books, which is more popular? Why?**
Although digital devices are ubiquitous, physical books still hold an undeniable charm and remain highly popular. Many book enthusiasts in Vietnam prefer the tactile sensation of turning pages and the distinct smell of paper, viewing physical books as collectible items. However, e-books are rapidly gaining traction among university students and busy professionals due to their sheer portability and cost-effectiveness, allowing readers to carry an entire library on a single tablet.

3. **What are the benefits of reading?**
Reading offers a multitude of cognitive and emotional benefits. Mentally, it provides superb cognitive stimulation, which keeps the brain active and can delay the onset of cognitive decline. Professionally, it systematically expands one's vocabulary and boosts linguistic prowess. On an emotional level, diving into fictional narratives fosters deep empathy, as it forces the reader to step into someone else's shoes and understand diverse human experiences.

4. **Why don’t many people read books?**
I believe the primary culprit is the sheer dominance of digital entertainment and the culture of instant gratification. With social media platforms offering short-form video content, people's attention spans have been severely fragmented. Many find the slow, focused process of reading a book too demanding when compared to the effortless, immediate dopamine hits provided by scrolling through their phones.

5. **Does reading help children develop?**
Absolutely. Reading is paramount during a child's formative years. Intellectually, exposure to books at an early age accelerates language acquisition, sharpens critical thinking, and stimulates creative imagination far better than passive screen time. Emotionally, storybooks help children navigate complex feelings, build moral compasses, and develop a healthy sense of empathy by observing how characters overcome life's obstacles.

- **Reason & Example (What we ate & talked about):** We indulged in a hotpot feast with a rich, savory broth and fresh organic ingredients. - **Alternative/Evaluation:** Had we decided to eat separately or order fast food at home, we would have missed out on this warm atmosphere and the opportunity to truly catch up and strengthen our social bonds.

### Part 3 Outline:
- Q1: Sharing meals is an ancient social ritual. It fosters a sense of belonging and allows people to build and strengthen social bonds.
- Q2: Highly beneficial but not always feasible nowadays. It is the ultimate quality time to maintain kinship, though busy schedules often get in the way.
- Q3: Advantages: Convenience, high-quality gastronomy, and no washing up. Disadvantages: Expensive, potentially less healthy, and can be noisy.

fields.sample:
### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **Do you work or are you a student?**
I am currently a university student, pursuing a degree in Software Engineering. It is a highly demanding field that requires a massive intellectual commitment, but building functional applications and solving complex coding issues is immensely rewarding.

2. **What kind of technology do you use most often in your daily life?**
My laptop and smartphone are undoubtedly the most ubiquitous pieces of technology in my daily routine. As a programmer, I rely on my high-performance laptop to write code and test software, while my phone helps me manage my schedule, communicate with peers, and streamline my workflow.

3. **Do you like buying shoes? How often do you buy them?**
I would not class myself as a compulsive shoe collector, but I certainly appreciate high-quality footwear. I typically purchase a new pair of shoes only twice or thrice a year, usually when my current pairs start showing signs of wear and tear.

4. **What is the most important thing for you when choosing a pair of shoes?**
For me, comfort and durability are absolutely paramount. Since I lead an active lifestyle and spend hours commuting, I always look for shoes with excellent arch support and ergonomic soles that literally make me feel like I am walking on air, rather than just choosing them for aesthetic appeal.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
I would like to tell you about a highly memorable dinner that I shared with a group of my closest friends from university last winter. We gathered at a cozy, rustic Vietnamese hotpot restaurant nestled in a quiet alleyway in the heart of Hanoi.

It was a chilly evening, which made the steaming pot of beef and mushroom hotpot we ordered exceptionally appealing. We indulged in a rich, savory broth packed with fresh beef slices, organic vegetables, and local tofu. As we sat around the bubbling pot, the conversation flowed completely naturally. We spent hours catching up on our latest academic struggles, particularly our grueling software development projects. We also took a trip down memory lane, laughing hysterically at some of the silly mistakes we made during our freshman year, and shared our future career aspirations after graduation.

I thoroughly enjoyed this dinner because it was the perfect antidote to our hectic academic schedules. The warm, inviting ambiance of the restaurant combined with the comfort of delicious food and genuine companionship was truly restorative. It reminded me of the importance of taking a step back from our busy lives to appreciate the people who support us through thick and thin.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **Why do people like to eat with others?**
Sharing a meal has always been a fundamental social ritual across human history. Eating together fosters a deep sense of community and belonging, allowing individuals to unwind and engage in meaningful conversations. It provides a relaxed, neutral setting where people can strengthen social bonds, share joy, and build lasting relationships.

2. **Is it important to have a meal with family members every day?**
While having a daily family meal is ideal, it may not always be feasible in this day and age due to conflicting work and school schedules. Nonetheless, it remains highly important. Gathering around the dinner table offers families a rare opportunity to have uninterrupted quality time, check in on each other's emotional well-being, and maintain a strong sense of kinship.

3. **What are the advantages and disadvantages of eating in restaurants?**
On the plus side, dining out offers unparalleled convenience, a diverse array of professional gastronomy, and spares people the tedious task of cooking and washing up. However, the drawbacks are also prominent. It is significantly more expensive than home-cooked meals, and commercial food often contains higher levels of sodium, sugar, and unhealthy fats, which can lead to health issues if consumed regularly.

4. **Do you think that the way people eat has changed in your country?**
Undoubtedly, the culinary habits in Vietnam have undergone a major paradigm shift. With the fast-paced nature of modern life, there is a noticeable rise in the consumption of fast food and processed meals. Moreover, the traditional practice of cooking elaborate family meals is gradually being replaced by the convenience of online food delivery services.

5. **How does technology affect the way we have dinner?**
Technology is a double-edged sword when it comes to dining. On one hand, mobile applications have made ordering food and reserving tables incredibly seamless. On the other hand, it has created the phenomenon of being 'digitally distracted' at the dinner table. People are often more engrossed in capturing photos for social media or scrolling through notifications than actively interacting with the companions sitting right in front of them.

### Part 1 Outline:
- Q1: High-quality matcha or Belgian dark chocolate. Bitter-sweet flavor profile, not overly sweet.
- Q2: Yes, a cherished childhood treat. Shared with family on hot summer days.
- Q3: The Siberian tiger. Majestic, solitary creature representing strength and environmental conservation.
- Q4: Only at national safari parks. Captivating yet humbling experience.

### Part 2 Outline (A.R.E.A):
- **Answer (Where, How far, When/How):** Svalbard, a remote Norwegian archipelago in the Arctic Ocean. Roughly 8000 kilometers from Hanoi. Plan to go during the summer months (for polar day) via multiple flights.
- **Reason & Example (Why visit & Activities):** I want to experience true, untouched pristine wilderness. Activities include dogsledding, viewing majestic glaciers, and hoping to safely observe polar bears in their natural habitat. It offers absolute silence and a complete escape from modern life.
- **Alternative/Evaluation:** Had I chosen a typical, crowded tourist destination like Paris or Tokyo, I would have faced sensory overload. Svalbard offers a profound sense of solitude that forces introspection and helps recharge my batteries completely.

### Part 3 Outline:
- Q1: To find a complete change of scenery and explore uncharted territory away from commercial tourism.
- Q2: Long holidays allow for deep mental rejuvenation. Short breaks often feel rushed, whereas long ones provide time to truly disconnect.
- Q3: To avoid the stress of travel logistics and financial costs, preferring to find peace in their own homes.
fields.sample:
### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **What is your favorite flavor of ice cream? Why?**
I have always had a bit of a sweet tooth, but my absolute favorite flavor is high-quality matcha or Belgian dark chocolate. I prefer these because they offer a complex, slightly bitter-sweet taste profile rather than the cloying sweetness of standard vanilla.

2. **Did you eat ice cream when you were a child?**
Most definitely. Eating ice cream is one of my most nostalgic childhood memories. During the sweltering summer months in Hanoi, my father would occasionally take me to the legendary Trang Tien ice cream parlor on his motorcycle, which was always an absolute highlight of my week.

3. **What is your favorite wild animal? Why?**
I am deeply fascinated by the Siberian tiger. It is a majestic, solitary apex predator that embodies raw strength and grace. Sadly, they are highly endangered, so they also represent the urgent need for global biodiversity conservation.

4. **Have you ever seen wild animals up close?**
Only in semi-wild environments like open safari parks. Seeing a pride of lions roaming relatively freely from the safety of a secure vehicle was a profoundly humbling experience that made me realize how magnificent these creatures are outside of cages.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
If I could choose any destination on Earth, I would love to visit Svalbard, a remarkably remote Norwegian archipelago situated in the freezing waters of the Arctic Ocean. Located roughly 8,000 kilometers away from my home in Hanoi, reaching this icy outpost would require an arduous journey, involving a flight to Oslo, followed by a domestic connection to Longyearbyen, the northernmost town on the planet.

I would ideally aim to travel there during the Arctic summer, around July or August, when the weather is relatively bearable and the region experiences the phenomenon of the midnight sun, meaning 24 hours of daylight. While there, I would love to participate in glacier hiking, navigate the deep fjords by boat, and experience dog-sledding across the tundra. My ultimate, albeit cautious, dream would be to safely witness polar bears or Arctic foxes in their natural, undisturbed habitat.

I am intensely drawn to Svalbard because it is literally in the middle of nowhere. In our hyper-connected, fast-paced modern world, I crave the absolute silence and raw, pristine beauty of the polar wilderness. There is an alluring sense of solitude there that I believe is impossible to find elsewhere. Standing amidst colossal glaciers and frozen fjords would allow me to completely disconnect, find mental clarity, and gain a profound appreciation for the fragile ecosystems of our planet.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **Why do many people like traveling to remote or faraway places?**
I believe the main catalyst is the pursuit of authentic novelty. Highly commercialized tourist spots often feel artificial and overcrowded. Travelers today increasingly seek off-the-beaten-path destinations to experience untouched landscapes, encounter distinct cultures, and push their personal boundaries in uncharted territory.

2. **Why is it beneficial for people to have long holidays rather than short ones?**
Long holidays are far superior for genuine mental rejuvenation. Short weekend getaways often feel incredibly rushed and can actually induce travel anxiety due to tight logistics. In contrast, a prolonged holiday allows an individual to truly disconnect from their workplace responsibilities, settle into a slower pace of life, and return to work with a fully restored cognitive capacity.

3. **Why do some people prefer to stay at home and relax during holidays?**
For many, traveling itself is an exhausting, high-stress endeavor involving expensive bookings, crowded airports, and packed itineraries. Individuals who lead highly demanding professional lives often find that a 'staycation'—staying in the comfort of their own home, reading books, or catching up on sleep—is the most effective way to recharge their batteries without the hassle of travel logistics.

### Part 1 Outline:
- Q1: Renting an apartment in Cau Giay, Hanoi. A bustling residential hub. Love the convenience, though it gets chaotic.
- Q2: FPT University has strict rules regarding attendance and dress codes. I prefer flexibility but understand they build self-discipline.
- Q3: Absolutely crucial. They act as an urban oasis, helping city dwellers escape air pollution and reconnect with nature.
- Q4: Weekly. I enjoy taking casual strolls in the local park to clear my head.

### Part 2 Outline (A.R.E.A):
- **Answer (What, When):** A natural aptitude for music, specifically having an ear for melody and pitch. Discovered this during my early childhood years when I could easily play back tunes on a toy piano without any formal sheet music.
- **Reason & Example (How to improve & Why):** I want to elevate this talent by taking professional masterclasses in software production and keyboard harmony. Since I study software engineering, combining technology with melody would allow me to produce my own music.
- **Alternative/Evaluation:** Without actively honing this skill, it remains a dormant, unutilized hobby. Polishing it could unlock new avenues for self-expression and perhaps a side career.

### Part 3 Outline:
- Q1: Yes, especially in physical or highly structured domains like mathematics, gymnastics, or music. Prodigies often show intuitive grasp before formal training.
- Q2: They tap into human curiosity, offer instant gratification, and provide an emotional rags-to-riches narrative that captivates audiences.
- Q3: Academic success offers a perceived safer, more predictable career path compared to the highly volatile and competitive creative industries.
- Q4: Absolutely. The immense pressure to live up to expectations can crush a person's mental well-being and strip away the joy of the activity itself.
fields.sample:
### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **Where is your living area? Do you like living there?**
I am currently renting an apartment in Cau Giay district, Hanoi, which is a highly dynamic residential hub. Personally, I absolutely adore it because of the unparalleled convenience; supermarkets, food stalls, and cafes are just a stone's throw away, though the traffic during rush hours can be rather chaotic.

2. **Are there many rules in your school or workplace? How do you feel about them?**
Yes, at FPT University, we have relatively strict policies regarding attendance tracking and assignment deadlines. While I occasionally find the administrative red tape slightly restrictive, I ultimately believe these regulations are necessary to instill self-discipline and keep us on track.

3. **Do you think it is important to have public parks and gardens in a city?**
Undoubtedly. Public green spaces serve as vital 'urban oases' amid concrete jungles. They offer local residents a dedicated space to escape suffocating exhaust fumes, engage in physical exercise, and reconnect with nature, which is paramount for psychological well-being.

4. **How often do you visit public parks or gardens?**
I try to make it a weekly habit. Every Sunday evening, I head to the local park to take a brisk walk. It is an exceptional way to declutter my mind, breathe in some fresh air, and prepare myself mentally for the grueling academic week ahead.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
I would like to talk about a natural talent that I have possessed since childhood, which is having a keen ear for music. From an early age, I realized I had a natural aptitude for identifying pitches and replicating melodies effortlessly. Whenever I heard a song on the radio, I could immediately play it back on a basic electronic keyboard without needing to look at any sheet music.

I first discovered this gift when I was around seven years old. My parents bought me a small toy piano, and within hours, I was playing simple traditional children's songs entirely by ear. While this intuitive grasp of melodies felt like second nature to me, I have never received formal classical training, which has kept my skills at a raw, unpolished level.

To elevate this talent to a professional standard, I intend to enroll in specialized music masterclasses, focusing on advanced keyboard harmony and digital audio workstation software. Because my academic major is software engineering, my dream is to integrate technology with my melodic intuition to produce ambient and electronic music.

I am incredibly eager to improve this talent because music is my ultimate emotional outlet. When I am stressed with coding or complex algorithms, sitting down at the keyboard and letting the notes flow allows me to completely decompress. I truly believe that while raw talent is a beautiful starting point, continuous practice is what turns a simple hobby into a profound, lifelong artistic medium.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **Do you think natural talent can be recognized at an early age?**
Yes, absolutely. In fields with clear structural patterns like mathematics, chess, or music, child prodigies often demonstrate an intuitive, almost inexplicable mastery long before receiving formal education. For instance, a child with a natural gift for athletics will inherently display superior coordination, spatial awareness, and physical agility compared to their peers.

2. **Why do you think talent competitions, like The Voice, have become so popular recently?**
I believe the massive appeal of these shows lies in their emotional narrative and relatability. Audiences are inherently drawn to rags-to-riches stories where ordinary people transform into superstars overnight. Furthermore, the interactive nature of these competitions, where viewers can vote, feeds into the modern craving for instant gratification and active participation.

3. **Why do some parents force their children to succeed academically instead of developing their natural talents?**
Historically, academic credentials have been viewed as a guaranteed ticket to financial stability and social status. Creative paths, such as music or painting, are often perceived as highly volatile and economically precarious. Therefore, out of protective instincts, parents push their children toward traditional professions like medicine, law, or engineering, valuing predictability over artistic fulfillment.

4. **Do you agree that having a natural talent can sometimes be a disadvantage or a burden to a person?**
I completely agree. Being labeled as exceptionally talented from a young age can be a heavy double-edged sword. It often places an immense psychological burden on an individual to constantly live up to lofty expectations. When people are praised solely for their innate abilities rather than their effort, they may develop a fear of failure, which can eventually paralyze their growth and strip away the pure enjoyment of their craft.

### Part 1 Outline:
- Q1: Student at FPT University studying Software Engineering. Demanding workload but highly rewarding when building apps.
- Q2: Not a big fan. I prefer sunny days as rain ruins outdoor plans and limits mobility.
- Q3: Navy blue. Used to love bright colors like yellow as a kid, but now lean towards sophisticated, calming tones.
- Q4: Absolutely. Warm colors stimulate energy, whereas cool tones like blue have a psychological calming effect.

### Part 2 Outline (A.R.E.A):
- **Answer (What, How, Who):** Organized a milestone 50th birthday party for my mother last year at a cozy boutique venue in Hanoi, with the assistance of my close family members.
- **Reason & Example (How we prepared):** We spent weeks secretly designing invitations, compiling a nostalgic video slideshow of her life, curating an acoustic playlist, and coordinating with a caterer for her favorite local dishes. My brother handled the technical setup while I managed the logistics.
- **Alternative/Evaluation:** If we hadn't planned ahead meticulously, the event would have been chaotic. Instead, seeing her genuinely moved to tears made it go off without a hitch, transforming it into a lifelong memory.

### Part 3 Outline:
- Q1: Parents must set a good example first. They can establish simple daily routines, encourage children to sort their toys, and use visual task boards to build organizational skills early.
- Q2: Major life milestones (weddings, corporate conferences, product launches) where tight timelines, large budgets, and multiple stakeholders are involved.
- Q3: Not necessarily. While career goals benefit from structure, over-planning stifles creativity and spontaneity. It is crucial to strike a balance and remain adaptive.

### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **Do you work or are you a student?**
I am currently a university student majoring in Software Engineering. It is a highly demanding field that requires endless hours of coding and logical problem-solving, but building mobile and web applications to streamline workflows makes the intellectual grind incredibly rewarding.

2. **Do you like rainy days? Why or why not?**
To be quite honest, I am far from being a pluviophile. I find rainy weather rather inconvenient as it severely limits my outdoor mobility, disrupts traffic, and dampens my overall productivity. I definitely prefer bright, sunny days that lift my spirits.

3. **What is your favorite color? Has this preference changed since you were a child?**
Currently, my absolute favorite color is navy blue because it exudes a sense of professionalism, depth, and calm. This is actually a major shift from my childhood, when I was drawn to highly vibrant, primary colors like red and bright yellow, which reflected a more energetic mindset.

4. **Do you think colors can affect a person's mood?**
Undoubtedly. Colors have a profound psychological impact on our subconscious mind. For instance, cool tones like green and blue are widely known to induce tranquility and relieve stress, whereas intense colors like red can stimulate passion, hunger, or even anxiety.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
I would love to tell you about a highly successful event that I organized last year, which was my mother’s milestone fiftieth birthday party. Since she has dedicated her entire life to raising my brother and me, we wanted to throw her a surprise celebration that she would cherish forever.

To make this happen, my brother and I began planning ahead nearly two months in advance. We booked a private room at a cozy boutique restaurant in Hanoi that featured a rustic interior. In terms of logistics, I took charge of coordinating the guest list of her closest high school friends, curating a custom acoustic music playlist, and working with the chef to design a menu of her favorite traditional Vietnamese dishes. Meanwhile, my brother compiled a heartwarming video slideshow showcasing precious family photographs over the decades, effectively taking her on a nostalgic trip down memory lane.

What made the event exceptionally successful was the element of surprise and the seamless execution. When my mother walked into the room under the pretense of a simple family dinner, only to be greeted by her dearest friends singing her favorite song, she was genuinely moved to tears. Thanks to our meticulous preparation, every segment of the evening went off without a hitch. The cozy ambiance, the laughter, and the heartfelt speeches created an atmosphere of pure joy, making all our hard work entirely worthwhile.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **How can parents help their children to become more organized?**
I believe the most effective way is for parents to set a good example through their own daily habits. Children are highly imitative; if they see their parents maintaining a tidy household, they will naturally follow suit. Additionally, parents can introduce structured routines early on, such as gamifying the process of cleaning up toys or utilizing colorful visual chore charts to teach time-management skills in a fun, engaging manner.

2. **On what occasions do people need to be highly organized?**
High levels of organization are absolutely critical during major life events and complex professional environments. For instance, planning a wedding, coordinating a massive corporate product launch, or preparing for high-stakes university examinations demand rigorous scheduling. On these occasions, dealing with multiple stakeholders, strict deadlines, and financial budgets leaves zero room for error.

3. **Does everything in life need to be meticulously planned and prepared?**
While structure is essential for achieving long-term professional goals, I do not believe every single facet of our existence should be rigidly calculated. Constantly over-analyzing and planning can induce unnecessary anxiety and completely stifle creativity. It is paramount to strike a healthy balance, leaving ample room for spontaneity and natural serendipity, which often lead to some of the most memorable experiences in life.

  * Practice smooth transitions for connected words: *went_off_without_a_hitch* /wentɒfwɪˈðaʊtəhɪtʃ/, *set_a_good_example* /setəɡʊdɪɡˈzɑːmpl/, *lift_my_spirits* /lɪftmaɪˈspɪrɪts/.
  * Be careful with the elision of the /t/ in fast speech: *next_month* sounds like /neksmʌnθ/.

- **Word Stress (Trọng âm từ):**
  * **Meticulous** /məˈtɪk.jə.ləs/ (primary stress is on the second syllable).
  * **Serendipity** /ˌser.ənˈdɪp.ə.ti/ (stress is on the third syllable).
  * **Logistics** /ləˈdʒɪs.tɪks/ (stress is on the second syllable).

- **Intonation (Ngữ điệu):**
  * When narrating a heartwarming moment in Part 2, slightly lower your pitch and soften your tone to show genuine emotional attachment: *"...she was **genuinely** moved to tears."*
  * Ensure a clear rising intonation on lists of items to signal more is coming: *"designing invitations [rising], compiling a nostalgic video [rising], and curating an acoustic playlist [falling]."*

### Part 1 Outline:
- Q1: Software Engineering student at FPT University. Highly demanding but rewarding when building apps.
- Q2: Laptop and smartphone. Laptop is indispensable for writing complex code, debugging, and running simulations.

### Part 2 Outline (A.R.E.A):
- **Answer (What, How long, What for):** A high-performance Dell XPS laptop, purchased about two years ago when starting university.
- **Reason & Example (Why useful):** It is my main workhorse. I use it for heavy software compiling, web development, and content creation. Its fast processing power and sleek ergonomic keyboard streamline my coding workflow immensely.
- **Alternative/Evaluation:** Had I relied solely on my phone or a low-end tablet, I would have struggled to execute heavy computational tasks, resulting in massive lag and delayed projects. This device is the backbone of my academic success.

### Part 3 Outline:
- Q1: Short-form videos offer instant gratification, which exploits the brain's dopamine reward system. Their highly personalized algorithms keep users hooked.
- Q2: Mass media (TV, newspapers) has a top-down, one-way communication model with strict editorial filters. Social media is decentralized, interactive, and user-generated.
- Q3: No, online learning cannot fully supplant physical classrooms. It lacks organic peer interaction, real-time collaboration, and the development of interpersonal skills. A hybrid model is the future.
fields.sample:
### Part 1 Sample Answers
1. **Where do you work or study?**
I am currently a university student at FPT University, where I am pursuing a degree in Software Engineering. It is an incredibly stimulating field that requires a great deal of analytical problem-solving, but being able to build functional programs and design mobile applications is exceptionally rewarding.

2. **What kind of technology do you use most often in your daily life?**
Apart from my smartphone, my laptop is undoubtedly the most ubiquitous piece of technology in my life. As a software engineering student, it is my absolute lifeline, as I use it daily to write code, design database architectures, and run heavy simulations.

3. **Do you prefer borrowing things or buying them?**
I generally prefer purchasing items rather than borrowing them, especially when it comes to technology or books. Buying gives me a sense of ownership, allows me to customize the item to my liking, and spares me the constant anxiety of accidentally damaging someone else's property.

### Part 2 Sample Answer
While smartphones are often considered the ultimate personal gadget, the most indispensable electronic device I own is my high-performance laptop, which I purchased about two years ago right before embarking on my university journey.

This device is a sleek, silver ultra-portable notebook, but despite its lightweight frame, it packs a massive computational punch. As a software engineering major, this laptop is my ultimate workhorse. I utilize it primarily to write complex code, run multi-threaded program simulations, and manage various web development projects. Additionally, it serves as my primary entertainment hub when I want to relax, allowing me to stream movies or edit high-definition video clips.

I believe this laptop is extraordinarily useful because it has completely streamlined my daily workflow. It boasts an ergonomic keyboard that makes typing for hours on end remarkably comfortable, and a long-lasting battery that allows me to work from anywhere without constantly hunting for power outlets. Without this device, managing my heavy academic workload and software projects would be next to impossible. It is not just a consumer electronics product; it is the vital gateway to my future career.

### Part 3 Sample Answers
1. **Why are so many young people obsessed with short videos on social media?**
I believe the primary culprit is the culture of instant gratification. Platforms like TikTok utilize highly sophisticated, proprietary algorithms that analyze user behavior in real time to feed them an endless stream of highly engaging, personalized content. These bite-sized videos, usually under a minute long, offer a rapid succession of dopamine hits, which unfortunately fragments the attention span of teenagers, making long-form content feel tedious by comparison.

2. **What are the key differences between mass media and social media platforms?**
There is a profound structural difference between the two. Traditional mass media, such as television networks and print newspapers, operates on a centralized, one-way broadcasting model where content is curated by professional editors and journalists, serving as a gatekeeper of information. Conversely, social media is highly decentralized and democratic, enabling user-generated content to spread globally instantly. It fosters bi-directional, highly interactive communication, allowing anyone to have a voice, though this often comes at the cost of journalistic integrity and the rapid spread of misinformation.

3. **Do you think online learning will eventually replace face-to-face classroom learning?**
Personally, I do not believe virtual learning will ever completely supplant traditional, physical classrooms. While online platforms offer unparalleled geographical flexibility and cost-effectiveness, they struggle to replicate the holistic pedagogical environment of a physical school. Face-to-face instruction facilitates natural, real-time collaboration, peer-to-peer mentoring, and the organic development of essential social and interpersonal skills. Therefore, the future of education will likely settle on a hybrid model rather than a total digital replacement.

  * Pay attention to the linking /r/ in *more_or_less* and *clear_and_concise*.

- **Word Stress (Trọng âm từ):**
  * **Proprietary** /prəˈpraɪə.tər.i/ (primary stress is on the second syllable).
  * **Pedagogical** /ˌped.əˈɡɒdʒ.ɪ.kəl/ (stress is on the third syllable).
  * **Computational** /ˌkɒm.pjʊˈteɪ.ʃən.əl/ (stress is on the fourth syllable).

- **Intonation (Ngữ điệu):**
  * When shifting from positive aspects to negative ones, use strong contrastive pitch changes: *"While online platforms offer **flexibility** [rising], they struggle to replicate **interpersonal connections** [falling]."*
  * Ensure a rising tone on items in series: *"write code [rising], design database architectures [rising], and run heavy simulations [falling]."*
